text: Every circuit you've simulated so far has run on a perfect, idealized machine. Real quantum hardware isn't perfect — qubits decohere, gates introduce small errors, and even the final measurement can misreport the result. Qiskit Aer lets you simulate those imperfections deliberately.

qiskit_aer.noise ships several error channel constructors, each modeling a genuinely different failure mode. depolarizing_error models a gate that, with some probability, gets replaced by a random Pauli error entirely. thermal_relaxation_error is more physically grounded: real T1 energy relaxation and T2 dephasing, as a function of how long a gate takes relative to the qubit's own T1 and T2. And readout_error models imperfection in the measurement step itself — a qubit truly in state 0 sometimes gets reported as 1. Unlike gate error, that's a purely classical distortion, which matters because it can potentially be corrected after the fact.

You don't need a real backend to experiment with noise. pauli_error with a 2% chance of X and 98% chance of identity, attached to every x gate, says: whenever an x gate runs, there's a 2% chance it actually gets an extra flip. Applied to a qubit prepared in |0> with no other gates, the true probabilities under this channel are P(0)=0.98 and P(1)=0.02.

Run that noisy circuit at 1024 shots and you get actual counts, not the exact 0.98/0.02 split — something like 0: 1000, 1: 24, an observed error rate around 2.34%. That's close to the injected 2%, but not exact, because the noise model injects a true probability of error, and the 1024 shots are a finite statistical sample of it. These are two separate, stackable sources of imperfection: the injected error itself, and ordinary sampling noise on top.

Hand-built noise models are useful for learning, but the real production pattern is pulling an actual backend's current calibrated noise characteristics directly into a simulation: NoiseModel.from_backend. This builds a model from the backend's live calibration data — its actual measured gate errors, T1/T2 times, and readout errors — giving you a realistic preview before spending real queue time on the hardware itself.
Next lesson looks closely at one of these three channels in particular: readout error, and why it's correctable in a way gate error fundamentally isn't.
